surfaces.SDK: the Go, Python and Java SDKs

promises.promise: Data goes to stdout and everything else to stderr; -o json prints clean data.
Every command that prints machine output accepts -o.
A usage error exits 2, in the CLI's own error style.
Every error says what happened, why, and what to do; stacks only in debug.
Off a terminal there is no colour, spinner or prompt, and NO_COLOR is honoured.
A headless run settles each approval by --approve-default, and denies when it is unset.
A destructive command confirms on a terminal; --force is the only bypass.
--help, version and completion never load the heavy modules.
get shows a view designed for each kind, and list fits the terminal.
Help groups commands and gives an example for each.
stigmer run ends the way its mode promises.
Provider keys are saved, listed and removed from the CLI.
A run's subagent rows show the right status and duration.
`stigmer up` says where the console is and whether agents can run.
A run's exit code says how its turn ended.
Global options work before or after the command.
`stigmer up` and `stigmer setup` check a model key with the provider before calling it ready, and on a terminal ask again when it is rejected.

A coding agent can take a newcomer from one prompt to their agent's chat in their own app: sign-in, an example or their own agent, a live key check with no key in the chat, a first run, and the app's route and chat.
A command the server refused ends with the server's help link when the server sets one.
Every state a run passes through has its own frame: loading, streaming, tools, approvals, file review, subagents, failure, completion.
An approval prompt is unmissable, keyboard-driven, and never times out into approval.
The published stigmer-ink starts with Node alone.
Off a terminal the session view renders read-only and never crashes.
A load failure says what was tried and what to do.
A host CLI starts a run and gets control back when it completes.
Esc stops a running turn and leaves the session usable.
The composer takes several lines, paste, and history.
A host CLI adds its own slash commands and @ completions.
Thinking shows, and a working indicator counts the time.
What is being written follows a terminal resize; what was written is never repeated.
Colours read on a light and a dark terminal: by default only status colours carry a hue, and a host's colours follow the background.
Long markdown (lists, code, tables) reads cleanly in the terminal.
The terminal kit installs without any browser package.
A host CLI passes its own colours; by default only status colours carry a hue.
A long turn never clears the terminal's scrollback or repeats what it already printed.
Leaving a session says the agent keeps working and how to come back.
The docs' terminal recordings are the terminal kit's own frames.
Every library installs from its packed tarball and imports under Node.
A strict TypeScript consumer compiles against every library's types.
No library entry grows past its size budget unnoticed.
Every TypeScript example in the docs compiles against the library it shows, or says why it cannot.
An app with only the peers on the React kit's install line imports the kit and builds.
The chat drops into an app as one component, within a size budget.
The look changes only on purpose: every hero screen matches an approved screenshot in light and dark.
Every hero screen passes the accessibility audit in light and dark.
While the agent works, the session says what it is doing, for how long, and how far it has got.
Everything a turn produced (an answer, a file, a change, a plan) opens from the conversation itself, with or without the inspector.
An end user or guest sees no builder controls (the engine, target and environment, usage, the inspector) unless the host adds them.
An approval waiting for the person is the most visible thing on the screen until it is answered, and Stop is always in reach while a turn can stop.
A finished session opens on what was asked, what was done and what came out, with its time, and its estimated cost for builders and reviewers.
At a 390-pixel column (a phone, a docked panel or a popup) every control of the chat is reachable and none covers another.
The panel and popup never trap focus or take a key the host uses, and closing the popup returns focus to what opened it.
The docs show the kit's parts live, drawn by the same code the screenshot check approves.
A message sent in a docs demo gets a scripted answer, never an error.
A turn's changed and made files appear once in the conversation, and only someone who may decide sees Undo.
The console never offers an act the server refuses.
A new person is led from sign-in to a provider key and a first answer.
The launcher says a provider is missing before a run fails; the model picker shows which models are ready.
Every settings page shares one shell, with its empty and loading states.
Type and spacing come from tokens; no text is smaller than the scale allows.
A new person's first screen asks what their agent should do for their users; one pick makes the agent and puts its sample and first message in front of them.
The key step says why, where to get a key, and checks it live; a rejected key is refused in plain words and an unchecked one is said.
After the first job, the console says what comes next and leads to making the agent theirs: change its instructions, run it on their own file, give it a skill.
Every action button is the kit's Button, IconButton or LinkButton, so every action in the console has one height, one size scale and one focus ring.

The console hands over what puts an agent in the builder's own app, for their stack, with their organization and agent filled in, makes what the route needs in place, and says when their app's first user arrives.
The console offers the coding-agent door from the first question, with its own address in the prompt.
The journey's last step brings the team in: the organization named, an invite link with its roles in plain words, who has joined; accepting lands the person in the organization.
Every console screen and every failure note offers the deployment's help link, or none when it sets none; a builder's app never shows it.
Clicking the Dock icon reopens a closed window.
Sign-in reads its identity provider from configuration.
Commands the app runs see the user's own PATH.
A notification opens the thread it is about.
The app shows whether agents are running on this computer, and offers Restart when they stopped.
Sign-in keys are kept in the system keychain, never in the app's web storage.
A server the app cannot reach, or one that offers no desktop sign-in, says so and how to choose another.
Every language quickstart ends by printing the agent's answer.
Examples show API keys as stk_.
Every Go, Python and Java example in the docs compiles against its SDK, or says why it cannot.
